title: Your syllabus needs an enemy
author: How to Teach With AI
source: How to Teach With AI, July 29, 2026
summary: This short piece argues that course syllabi are approved by a committee of one—the author—and therefore never receive the hostile stress-testing they need before real students exploit their weaknesses. The solution is a three-reader AI prompt that simulates a grade-focused student hunting for loopholes, a skeptical senior colleague critiquing toothless policies, and an overwhelmed first-generation student flagging assumed knowledge. The prompt instructs each reader to list five sharp objections with the exact triggering line, then collectively identify the three changes that would defuse the most objections at once. The author claims this ten-minute exercise catches problems that would otherwise surface as email threads in October, and that the first-generation reader reliably catches assumptions invisible to the author who wrote the document decades ago. The underlying principle is that nothing student-facing should ship without a hostile read first—the same quality assurance reflex should extend to rubrics and final exam instructions.
points: Syllabi are approved by a committee of one (the author) and then read by students as opposing counsel hunting for loopholes, policy contradictions, and vague language exploitable in week twelve.

A three-reader AI prompt—grade-focused student, skeptical senior colleague, overwhelmed first-generation student—surfaces objections before the real audience arrives, preventing the costly email threads that follow.

The first-generation reader reliably catches assumptions invisible to the instructor who wrote the document for a student they stopped being decades ago—assumptions about background knowledge, process familiarity, and what 'obvious' means.
Three readers is a start; a full simulated committee that argues with each other produces even sharper catches than individual readers reviewing in isolation.
The reflex is the point: run the hostile-read prompt on every student-facing document—syllabus, rubric, final exam instructions—as a standard pre-launch quality check.
quotes: Every document in my course was approved by a committee of one. I wrote the syllabus, I revised the syllabus, I approved the syllabus. Same committee every time. It has never once sent my work back.

Students are not that committee. They read the syllabus like opposing counsel: hunting the late-policy loophole, the contradiction between page 2 and the LMS, the assignment description vague enough to argue about in week 12.

'You are three readers reviewing my syllabus, and none of you are being polite. Reader 1 is a grade-focused student hunting for loopholes, contradictions, and anything vague enough to dispute later. Reader 2 is a skeptical senior colleague who thinks my policies are either toothless or theatrical, and says which. Reader 3 is an overwhelmed first-generation student who flags every place the document assumes knowledge nobody gave them.'

It takes ten minutes. You'll fix two things before fall that would cost you a bunch of email threads in October, and the first-gen reader will catch something that's been invisible to you for years, because you wrote the document for a student you stopped being decades ago.
The reflex is the point: nothing student-facing ships without a hostile read first.
Borrow a trick from every other craft: get a hostile read before the real audience arrives.
